title: Leisure's Share in the Nation's Expenditure
aiDescription: The figure compares Britain’s personal expenditure in 1938 and 1945 across leisure-related categories and footwear. It uses two stacked pictorial bar groups made of circles, with green, blue, and black filled circles against gray outlines to show amounts for drink, smoking, reading matter, entertainment, travel, and footwear.

title: Youth Clubs in the City of Nottingham
aiDescription: Two related charts compare youth-club expenditure and the formation of youth clubs in Nottingham across several years. The left chart uses colored circles along horizontal rows to show spending categories, while the right chart uses grouped vertical bars in red and blue to show the number of clubs started each year, with small club icons across the top.

title: Public Libraries in Great Britain
aiDescription: The figure compares public library activity in Great Britain for urban libraries and county libraries in 1924 and 1939. It uses grouped pictorial bars arranged in two side-by-side panels, with repeated black, blue, gray, and red symbols to encode borrowers, issues, books in stock, and shillings spent per 10 people.

title: BBC Programmes. Size of Audiences, 1947
aiDescription: The figure compares the size of audiences for several BBC programmes in 1947. Audience levels are shown with rows of red and gray human symbols arranged beside each programme, with red indicating listening and gray indicating others, alongside a central radio tower with concentric broadcast rings.

title: Football Ground as a Recreation Centre
aiDescription: The figure compares a football ground with a proposed recreation centre that adds leisure, housing, and service facilities around the pitch. It is shown as a split layout with a 3D building view on the left and a labeled plan on the right, using green for the field and red, blue, and gray blocks for the surrounding amenities.

title: Middlesbrough: Present and Proposed Leisure Facilities and Services
aiDescription: The figure compares present and proposed leisure facilities and neighbourhood services for Middlesbrough. It is shown as two side-by-side chart maps of the same area, using colored background regions and small colored square symbols to encode different land uses and service types.

title: The Soviet Union's Foreign Trade with Britain and U.S.A.
aiDescription: The figure compares the Soviet Union’s foreign trade with Britain, the United States, and other countries in 1935 and 1938. It uses two green triangular panels with national symbols and groups of red, blue, and black arrows pointing inward or outward to encode import and export amounts.

title: Each exports what the other needs
aiDescription: The figure compares the total net imports and exports of Great Britain and the Soviet Union by broad commodity type, showing which side had import or export surpluses. It uses paired vertical panels with colored horizontal arrows and small product icons, where solid arrows point from a column and outlined arrows point into a column, with green for foodstuffs, blue for materials, and red for manufactured articles.

title: How Soviet Industry buys Foreign Equipment
aiDescription: This diagram explains the step-by-step process by which Soviet industry buys foreign equipment, from a steel trust’s request through approvals, supplier selection, ordering, and final delivery. The information is encoded as a horizontal flow diagram with numbered stages, red arrows and symbols showing the sequence, and a green shaded Soviet Union section contrasted with an unshaded Abroad area.

title: Mountain Chains and Main Water Communications of South-East Europe
aiDescription: A map compares the mountain chains and main water communications of South-East Europe, centering the Danube Valley and its river traffic. It uses a stylized relief map with shaded mountain bands, light blue water routes, black place markers, and a compass that shows north pointing to the right.
originalCaption: This map is presented from an unusual aspect. North is to the right instead of at the top. The idea is to show the Danube Valley as the centre of the chart. The reader is looking up stream from the mouth of the river. The Danubian basin appears to be cut in two parts, connected only by the Iron Gate. It will be seen that the more important outlet to the Hungarian plain is southward to Salonika. The distribution of black symbols along the course of the Danube indicates the relative density of river traffic.

title: Railways and Secondary Roads
aiDescription: The figure compares railways and secondary roads in Denmark and Danubia, alongside urban and rural population counts. It uses red and green pictorial unit lines and stacked train, horse-cart, and tractor symbols laid out in two labeled horizontal sections.
originalCaption: Each man represents one-tenth of the total population. Red: urban. Green: rural. Each unit of length represents 1 metre of transport route for every 10 people. Red: railways. Green: secondary roads.

title: Food Production and Consumption
aiDescription: The figure compares food production and consumption in Denmark and Danubia, showing how much food one agricultural worker can produce and how much is exported or lacking for the home population. It is laid out as a pictorial unit chart with red worker symbols, green food sacks, blue arrows, and boxed stacks arranged in two country sections on a light background.
originalCaption: FOOD PRODUCTION AND CONSUMPTION IN DENMARK-modern farming methods enable one agricultural worker to produce enough food for 4 people. Three-fourths of the total produced can therefore be exported. IN DANUBIA—one agricultural worker produces food for only 1½ people. But 50 per cent of the food produced is exported, leaving a 25 per cent deficiency for the home population.

title: Cross Sections of the Danube Valley
aiDescription: The figure compares cross sections of the Danube Valley from north to south, showing how mountains, valleys, vegetation, cities, and waterways change along the river. The information is encoded as a stylized map with stacked horizontal landscape bands, a blue river line, red city symbols, brown mountain and woodland icons, and green grassland or cropland areas over a pale geographic base.

title: Infant Mortality
aiDescription: This map compares infant mortality rates across several European countries, with darker shading indicating higher percentages. The countries are shown as a choropleth map with labeled regions and a four-step gray-to-black key beneath the map.

title: Deaths of Infants Under One Year 1938
aiDescription: The figure compares infant deaths under one year in 1938 across several European countries, showing relative mortality levels. It uses rows of orange infant icons paired with black cross symbols, arranged in two columns with country names above each row and a note that each cross represents 1 death per 100 live births.

title: Water Power—Used and Unused
aiDescription: The figure compares potential and actual water power across several Central and Southeastern European countries. It uses a political map with repeated blue waterfall icons to represent potential hydraulic power and small red arrows to mark power in actual use.

title: The altitudes of South-East Europe
aiDescription: This figure shows the altitude distribution of South-East Europe, emphasizing how mountain ranges and plains vary in elevation across the region. It is presented as a shaded relief map with layered color bands for height, blue rivers and seas, labeled mountain ranges and countries, plus a small stepped altitude diagram and compass for orientation.
originalCaption: Altitudes are an important factor in the development of water power. Rivers running down mountain slopes can feed electric power stations and drive water mills and other devices which help man in his work. The steeper the gradient, the more forceful the fall of water; the greater the bulk of water, the more power available.

title: Changing Industry
aiDescription: The figure compares successive stages of industrial production, from handcraft workshops to factories powered by steam, electricity, diesel, and an uncertain future stage. It is arranged as a vertical sequence of boxed panels using small worker-and-machine symbols, colored power and transport icons, and a large question mark in the final panel.
originalCaption: Hand-craftsmen in their own workshops gave place to factory-workers with steam-powered, belt-driven machinery. Electric power made it possible for machines to have individual motors, driven from local electricity-supply. Diesel engines, using coal converted into oil, gave power to isolated workshops, dependent however on the limitations of transport to maintain the fuel-supply. Atomic engines, self-contained and self-sustaining, can make industries "foot-loose" —geographically unfettered by natural power-resources.

title: Tomorrow's Energy ... and Today's
aiDescription: The figure compares the energy value of coal and uranium, showing how a tiny amount of uranium-235 is represented as enormously greater than an equal weight of coal. It uses isometric cube and square-like blocks in gray, red, and orange, with a large orange array of dots/tiles for atomic energy and smaller labeled blocks for pitchblende, uranium ore, U235, and coal laid out across the spread.
originalCaption: A comparison of the energy-values of coal and uranium. Uranium ore, obtained from pitchblende, consists of both U235 and U238. For every 140 parts of U238 is found one part of U235 which produces uranium fission and releases atomic energy. U235 is capable of releasing more than a million times as much energy as its equal weight of coal. Expressed in terms of equal weights of pitchblende and coal (see above), atomic energy is represented as 10,000 dots to the single speck of coal-energy. Extraction of uranium ore from ditchblende and the isolation of U235 from the ore involve elaborate and expensive processes and vast industrial pants and the atomic engine for converting energy into a motive power is still very primitive. In time it will be improved and atomic energy will be widely available.

title: Industrial Resources of Today
aiDescription: The figure compares the distribution of iron and coal resources across the world by continent. It is encoded as a world map with blue and black stacked symbols placed over each region, using more symbols to indicate larger resource totals.
originalCaption: The atomic engine, when perfected, will be self-supporting. Areas of the world which have remained undeveloped because of remoteness from sources of coal or oil or hydro-electric power will be opened up. Chart below (left), shows the distribution of iron and coal resources according to continents. Each blue symbol represents 5,000,000,000 tons of iron and each black symbol represents 250,000,000,000 tons of coal. Hitherto the distribution of industry has coincided with the distribution of iron and coal.

title: Industrial Development of Today
aiDescription: A world map compares industrial development across regions by showing how many people are associated with modern industry versus older or primitive forms of production. The information is encoded with small human symbols placed over continents, using red, blue, and green figures on a blue map background to represent different development stages.
originalCaption: The right-hand chart expresses, in terms of population, the relative stages of development to-day. Each symbol represents 50,000,000 population. Red stands for modern industry; blue for ancient forms of handicraft and green for primitive forms. so while 750,000,000 people have been aftected by modern industry 1,200,000,000 have remained outside its influences. Atomic energy can provide motive power for industry anywhere. It will provide power sources for peoples now dependent on handcrats. It will open up new areas for agricultural development and raise the living standard of people everywhere. Plastics from growing plants and light metals which are scattered over the surface of the globe will be developed and will completely change the world pattern dictated by the coal-iron economy. Atomic dower can be used to move mountains, change river courses or create great dams. By changing contours it can even alter climate. So there's hope for us yet!

title: Why Neutrons?
aiDescription: The figure explains how neutrons interact with atoms and why they are useful for triggering nuclear chain reactions and heavy-water moderation. It uses a sequence of framed schematic panels with colored dots, arrows, and labeled uranium nuclei to show particle paths, collisions, and fission events, alongside explanatory text blocks.

title: The Structure of the Foreign Office
aiDescription: A diagram shows the organizational structure of the Foreign Office and how its central departments connect to regional departments around the world. The relationships are encoded with labeled boxes and connecting lines above a colored world map that shades each region by department.
originalCaption: At the top and right-hand side are the functional and administrative departments; across the bottom are the nine regional departments and also "Communications" which serves the whole organisation.

title: The Northern Department of the Foreign Office and its Missions Abroad
aiDescription: The figure compares the Foreign Office’s Northern Department with its missions abroad across several countries, showing the staffing and diplomatic roles associated with each location. It is encoded as a labeled organizational diagram with boxed columns, connecting lines, and repeated person icons in blue, green, and red, with outline symbols and a small legend explaining the color and symbol meanings.
originalCaption: Those serving in regional departments are not specially chosen for their personal knowledge of the countries concerned, but for experience in dealing with diplomatic problems on Foreign Office lines. When this chart was compiled only one of the permanent officials in the Northern Department had been stationed in a capital concerned.

title: World Films and Filmgoers
aiDescription: The figure compares world film production, cinema capacity, and weekly filmgoers for the United States, Great Britain, and the rest of the world. It uses stacked pictorial bars with blue, red, and gray symbols arranged in groups, with different icon shapes indicating reels, screens, seats, and audience size.

title: Monopolies of the British Film Industry
aiDescription: The figure compares how much U.S. interests penetrate different parts of the British film industry, with a special emphasis on independent units versus companies under U.S. influence. It uses a horizontal pictorial bar layout with colored blocks and film-strip symbols arranged in rows, with a large blue USA bar at left and labeled sections such as Rank and ABC inside a red-outlined frame.
originalCaption: Symbols on the left represent independent units. U.S. interests penetrate the Rank Organisation and the A.B.C. group in varying degrees-up to 37½% in the latter. Only independents are outside the U.S. sphere—there are no independent all-British newsreels.

title: London's West End Cinemas
aiDescription: The figure compares seating capacity and ownership of London’s West End cinemas, showing U.S. interests, the Rank organisation, and independent owners. It uses a small location map at the top and a pictorial capacity chart below with colored blocks and seat symbols, where blue marks U.S. interests, orange and blue mark Rank, and black marks independent owners.
originalCaption:
The symbols on the white ground represent seats in independently owned cinemas. Note that the A.B.C. group has no seats in the West End In addition to their own, American interests have a
large stake in the Rank cinema circuits. The independent cinemas are almost all very small (under 600 seats) and five or six concentrate on foreign language films.

title: Financial Structure of United States Film Industry
aiDescription: The diagram compares the financial structure of the United States film industry, contrasting costs of production with income from rentals and foreign or domestic sources. It uses horizontal arrows of equal unit value between a studio icon, a central U.S. film industry block, and labeled source bands, all drawn in black on a simple schematic layout.

title: United Kingdom Food Requirements for 1945
aiDescription: The figure compares United Kingdom food requirements for 1945 across several food groups, showing how home production, imports, and deficiencies contribute to the total. It is encoded as a pictorial diverging bar chart with rows of food symbols, using green for home produce, solid blue for imported amounts, and outline blue for deficiencies, split around a central vertical divider.

title: Daily Milk Sales in England and Wales
aiDescription: The figure compares daily milk sales in England and Wales across several periods, including an average, wartime years, and a 1950 target. It uses rows of pictorial bottles and people as a unit bar chart, with green, red, and blue encoding different uses and a blue shaded block emphasizing milk distributed through national and school schemes.

title: Milk Retailer's margin
aiDescription: The figure compares the milk retailer’s margin by showing how it is divided among processing and bottling, distribution, administration, and interest on capital and profit. A pair of vertical symbol columns uses colored round markers and pictograms to encode the amounts, with one column representing the breakdown and the other a simplified comparison.

title: Two Ways of Farming a Hundred Acres
aiDescription: A comparison of two ways of farming a hundred acres, contrasting a mixed arable-and-dairy farm with a specialist dairy farm. The information is encoded as two large symbolic farm maps stacked vertically, with colored land parcels and icons for livestock, crops, labor, equipment, imports, and sales shown in side panels on the right.
originalCaption: Above: a mixed arable and dairy farm growing cereal and vegetables for sale as well as for the maintenance of a small herd of cows. This farm uses no imported cattle food. Below: a specialist dairy farm on which the grass is managed scientifically and additional feeding stuff is imported. Compare the equipment, labour and sales.

title: The Pattern of British Farming
aiDescription: The figure compares British farming patterns in 1930–35 and 1950–55, showing how livestock, cereals, and grassland regions are distributed and how they may change over time. Two side-by-side maps use colored land zones, diagonal stripes, boundary lines, and small animal symbols to encode rainfall bands, crop and pasture types, and cattle, sheep, and poultry concentrations.
originalCaption:
Of the physical factors that condition British farming systems the most important are rainfall and temperature. The left-hand map shows the counties which had the highest concentrations of cattle and sheep in the 1930's, and the largest acreages both of the principal cereals and of temporary and permanent pastures. The dividing line between oats and the other cereals was determined by the summer temperature; rainfall determined the boundary between permanent and temporary grass. Pigs and poultry have been omitted as they were maintained almost entirely on imported feeding stuffs.
The right-hand map shows the way in which British agriculture is likely to develop during the next 25 years. The new varieties of grass produced by plant-breeders have made the old boundaries out-of-date. A general extension of grazing leys would make it possible to double the pre-war output of milk without importing more feeding stuffs. Pigs could also be largely maintained on home-grown food.

title: Growth of Coventry
aiDescription: A comparison of Coventry’s growth and boundary expansion from 1890 to 1945, alongside the city’s rising population. The information is encoded with four stacked map-like city outlines in different shaded patterns and matching rows of boxed human figures, all in black and white, with years labeled beside each row.
originalCaption: Coventry's boundaries have been enlarged four times since 1890, while the population has grown fivefold. The time has come when simply adding new administrative districts to the outside edges of the city is just not enough–re-organisation must start from the centre and be drastic in its methods.

title: More Births and Fewer Deaths
aiDescription: The figure compares births and deaths across 1937-38, 1940-41, and 1944, showing that births increased while deaths decreased over time. It is a pictorial horizontal bar chart that uses red baby icons for births and gravestone icons in black and gray for deaths, arranged in separate rows for each year.

title: Coventry at Work
aiDescription: The figure compares Coventry’s workforce by industry across 1935, 1939, and 1941, highlighting the dominance of one industrial group and the smaller number of workers supplying local goods and services. It is encoded as a pictorial horizontal bar chart with rows of person symbols and industry icons, using red, blue, black, and green grouped by labeled sectors and year.
originalCaption: Coventry depends for its prosperity on one group of industries, shown in red. There are only the workers shown in green to provide Coventry people with goods and services.

title: Integration—and Disintegration
aiDescription: The figure compares the integration and disintegration of cotton textile operations across several mills and departments, showing how work is distributed and combined. It uses labeled process boxes and stacked pictorial bars made of colored worker icons, with green, blue, red, orange, and gray groups laid out in horizontal rows and tall vertical columns.

title: Tootal's Production Pipelines
aiDescription: A production-flow diagram compares the stages and decisions involved in making Tootal products, from designs and research through sales, production management, production, and testing. The process is encoded with labeled boxes, arrows, and a thick blue winding pipeline that traces the route through the stages, with simple pictograms and gray background panels for each step.
originalCaption: This chart shows how a Tootal product comes into being. The production manager is the key man, but every material must pass the testing department-two out of every three samples are rejected. Designs come partly from outside studios, all other stages shown here are within the Tootal organisation. Ties, handkerchiefs, dresses, dressing-gowns and piece goods are sent all over the world.

title: Half a Century of World Sugar
aiDescription: A historical infographic compares world sugar production across several time periods and regions, showing how the balance shifted among the British Empire, Europe, America, and the rest of the world. The information is encoded as stacked pictorial columns and horizontal rows of repeated cane symbols with colored segments, connected by gray lines and accompanied by small inset illustrations and explanatory text.

title: World Sugar Market 1938-39
aiDescription: The figure compares the world sugar market in 1938–39, showing where sugar was produced, consumed, imported, and shipped between major regions. A gray world map is overlaid with green sugar symbols, blue and red outlined rectangles, and curved solid or dashed flow lines that trace trade routes between labeled regions.

title: Caribbean Sugar in the World Market
aiDescription: The figure compares Caribbean sugar production and how it is distributed to different markets, showing amounts consumed at home and exported under protected or free-market trade. It uses a pictorial unit-area layout with stacked symbols and connecting lines between country boxes and destination boxes, with green, blue, and red coding for the three categories.

title: Settlement in Australia
aiDescription: The figure compares the settlement and population growth of Australia from early colonisation through the mid-20th century, highlighting major migration, transport, and economic milestones. It uses a black-and-white timeline with pictorial symbols and a small series of outline maps showing the spread of settlement across Australia over time.
originalCaption: The first sixty years of colonisation saw rapid expansion on all sides: the white population increased from 1,019 in 1788 to 405,500 in 1850. From Sydney, Europeans gradually infiltrated west, north and south. The discovery in 1813 of a way over the Blue Mountains into the interior of New South Wales led to expansion of the wool-growing industry. In 1834, sheep farmers from Tasmania, settling in what is now Victoria, had soon occupied a thousand miles of country stretching north to the Queensland border, while two years later settlers from England founded South Australia. In the 1840's free or assisted migration from the British Isles brought more immigrants so that by 1850 a belt of settlement extended from Rockhampton in Queensland to Spencer Gulf.

title: Australia, Vegetation and Water Supply
aiDescription: The figure compares Australia’s vegetation, rainfall, and water-supply features across regions. It uses a colored thematic map with rainfall bands, overlaid symbols for land use, livestock, towns, mountains, rivers, dams, and irrigation systems, plus a small comparison bar at the bottom.

title: Britain's Commodity Exports must increase by 75 per cent—Why?
aiDescription: A comparison chart explains why Britain’s commodity exports would need to rise by 75 percent, contrasting pre-war imports and the sources used to pay for them with a later scenario after imports recover and foreign debts must be repaid. The information is encoded as clustered circles in an area-chart layout with ship icons and arrows, using green, red, blue, yellow, gray, and black groups to show different payment categories and the added deficit or required increase.

title: Commodities Exported
aiDescription: The figure compares exports of different commodities before the war, during the last year of the war, and after the war target. It uses stacked rows of colored circular pictorial symbols and solid dots to show quantities for each commodity group, with a key at the bottom matching colors and icons to goods types.
originalCaption: Exports of food, coal and other raw materials, textiles, and iron and steel are not likely to show much increase over pre-war. This means that the deficiency in these will have to be made up from other goods such as those shown on the right. The reduced wartime exports emphasise the vastness of the post-war target.

title: The British Market
aiDescription: The figure compares British and other countries’ import markets in 1938, with a focus on the size of imports for countries such as the Empire, France, Germany, the U.S.A., and the rest of the world. It uses stacked pictorial crates arranged in horizontal bars, with colored rows and a bracketed grouping on the left to show relative import volumes by region and country.
originalCaption: One-half of British pre-war exports went to Empire countries; in some they accounted for up to 50 per cent of total imports. British exports to these countries can only be increased if their total import capacity is increased. Possible new markets include Russia, which took less than one per cent of British pre-war exports.

title: Trade in Electrical Goods, average 1936–38
aiDescription: The figure compares trade in electrical goods in 1936–38, showing British exports and the import sources of Argentina and South Africa. It uses a black flow diagram with boxes, arrows of varying length, and country symbols to encode trade direction and magnitude.

title: World Market for Bicycles
aiDescription: The figure compares the world market for bicycles before and after the war, showing exports from Britain, Germany, Japan, and France. It uses rows of bicycle icons and connecting flow lines in a black-and-white diagram, with each bicycle standing for 10 percent of the world market.

title: World Exports 1938
aiDescription: The figure compares world exports in 1938 across regions and countries, showing how export value is distributed among America, Europe, the U.S.S.R. and Far East, and the Rest of the World. It is a black pictorial bar chart arranged in four boxed panels, with repeated crate symbols representing equal export units and labels beside each category.

title: Reuters' Transmission of News
aiDescription: The figure maps the workflow of Reuters news transmission from incoming teleprinters through editorial handling and regional revisions to outgoing services around the world. It uses a process diagram with curved red flow bands, small worker and machine icons, and colored blocks arranged across the composition to show the sequence and branching routes.
originalCaption: The London headquarters of Reuters is the nerve centre of a world-wide organisation for the exchange of news. Chart shows the twelve teleprinters delivering their stream of telegrams which are read by an editor, known as a copy taster, who directs sub-editors as to the length and treatment of each news item.

title: Reuters' Main Office, Bureaux, Correspondents; Details for Europe and Mediterranean
aiDescription: The figure compares Reuters’ main offices, bureaux, and correspondents worldwide, with a detailed inset for Europe and the Mediterranean. Locations are encoded on outlined world and regional maps using colored symbols: red for main offices, blue for bureaux, and green for correspondents, arranged as clustered markers across the map areas.
originalCaption: Messages from Reuter offices and correspondents all over the world reach London over the regular commercial cable channels and are relayed by teleprinter to Reuters' Fleet Street office. Nearly a third of the wordage received is rejected by the copy taster (see page 61), who must have a complete grasp of current affairs and an ability to assess news value, as well as a knowledge of the requirements of the world-wide list of Reuter subscribers.

title: Productivity of Land, 1938; Electricity Output by Regions and large Towns, 1939
aiDescription: The figure compares land productivity in different parts of Italy in 1938 and electricity output by regions and large towns in 1939. The left panel uses boxed rows of green wheat symbols to compare yield, while the right panel uses an outline map of Italy with red lightning symbols for electricity and black town icons for population markers.
originalCaption: It is usual to talk of the "Agricultural South" of Italy, but productivity of the land is actually higher in the North. This is due partly to the natural fertility of the soil; partly to the cheap supply of electricity from highly developed hydro-electric schemes. These facilitate modern irrigation systems and enable industry to provide better farm machinery which is so urgently needed.

title: Italian Emigrants seeking Work
aiDescription: The figure compares annual average Italian emigration across five periods from 1876 to 1938, showing a rise to a peak before a steep decline. It uses rows of man icons as a pictorial bar chart, with blue and yellow backgrounds and wavy baselines to distinguish destinations, alongside a large silhouette map of Italy.
originalCaption: Italy's population (146.9 to the square kilometre) is steadily rising; by 1970 will reach maximum of about 50 millions. Up to 1915 mass emigration alleviated Italy's demographic problem-peak year was 1913, with over 872,000 emigrants. Slumps and quota restrictions abroad reduced this flow to a trickle. Emigration to Italian colonies was negligible, required heavy subsidies. Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Brazil and France have some room-will they welcome Italians?

title: Agricultural Land and Ownership
aiDescription: The figure compares how Italy’s agricultural land in 1930 was divided among North, Centre, and South/Islands, and among large estates, medium estates, and small holdings. It is encoded as a pictorial grid with green square blocks for area, black house symbols for large estates, blue house symbols for medium estates, and red house symbols for small holdings, arranged in horizontal rows by region with explanatory text on the right.
originalCaption: The chart shows how in 1930 over 25,000,000 hectares of farm land in Italy were divided between North, South and centre, and between estates, large, small and medium. The same total can be broken down roughly as follows: one-tenth owned by ecclesiastical bodies; one-fifth, other public bodies; one-ninth, titled families; one-twenty-sixth, banks and companies; one-thirteenth "capitalist peasants"; one-third, other "bourgeois" interests; one-eighth, medium peasants; one-tenth, small and poor peasants; and one fifteenth, allotments.
